100+ Best Resume Action Verbs (2026)

Replace passive phrases like 'responsible for' with high-impact power verbs proven to pass ATS algorithms and impress recruiters.

MV
Marcus Vance (Senior Career Coach) Nov 28, 2026 • 8 min read

When hiring managers scan your resume, they spend an average of 7.4 seconds conducting initial triage. During those crucial seconds, passive phrases like 'responsible for', 'assisted with', or 'worked on' fail to capture attention. They describe a job description rather than your personal achievements.

In 2026, automated Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) like Workday, Greenhouse, Taleo, and Lever use Natural Language Processing (NLP) vector embeddings to score candidate competency. Resumes that open bullet points with decisive, metric-oriented action verbs score higher for leadership and domain mastery.

Before refining your vocabulary, make sure you have organized your essential resume sections and verified your document formatting using our best resume format guide.

The Formula: Action Verb + Project + Quantified Impact

The strongest resume bullets follow the proven Google X-Y-Z formula:

"Accomplished [X], as measured by [Y], by leading [Z]."

Every strong bullet point starts with an active past-tense verb that defines your exact ownership:

Weak / Passive BulletHigh-Impact Action Verb Rewrite
Responsible for managing customer support tickets.Resolved 1,450+ client inquiries maintaining a 98.7% CSAT score, reducing average ticket turnaround time by 34%.
Worked on backend database speed.Refactored PostgreSQL indexing layers, slashing query latency by 58% for 12,000 active daily platform users.
Helped marketing team run social ads.Orchestrated multi-channel LinkedIn acquisition campaign, generating 420 qualified B2B leads and $85K ARR in Q2.
Was in charge of onboarding new engineers.Mentored 6 junior software engineers, accelerating production deployment ramp-up time from 6 weeks to 18 days.

1. Leadership, Management & Strategy Power Verbs

Use these verbs when demonstrating executive direction, team empowerment, project orchestration, and resource stewardship:

  • Spearheaded — Initiated and drove a major project from ideation to delivery.
  • Orchestrated — Coordinated multiple stakeholders or complex initiatives across departments.
  • Mobilized — Galvanized resources and teams around a tight deadline or emergency sprint.
  • Championed — Advocated for a cultural, technical, or procedural shift that drove measurable outcomes.
  • Pioneered — Introduced a groundbreaking strategy or architecture not previously attempted.
  • Steered — Navigated an organization or unit through market transitions or restructuring.
  • Consolidated — Merged disparate systems, reducing operational overhead.
  • Delegated — Assigned responsibilities effectively to scale team capacity and bandwidth.
  • Fostered — Built a collaborative environment that improved employee retention or velocity.
  • Restructured — Reorganized workflows to eliminate redundancies and bottleneck delays.

Example: Spearheaded cross-functional migration of legacy billing systems to Stripe, cutting churn by 18% and reclaiming 24 hours of monthly engineering maintenance.

2. Technical, Engineering & Development Power Verbs

When applying for software engineering, DevOps, data architecture, or IT roles, choose verbs that convey exact technical execution rather than generic participation:

  • Architected — Designed high-level system structures, databases, or cloud infrastructures.
  • Engineered — Built robust, scalable software, hardware, or algorithmic solutions.
  • Refactored — Improved existing codebases without altering external behavior to enhance speed or readability.
  • Automated — Replaced repetitive manual workflows with automated scripts or CI/CD pipelines.
  • Containerized — Packaged applications with Docker and Kubernetes for consistent cloud deployment.
  • Provisioned — Configured cloud infrastructure, clusters, or database instances via Terraform.
  • Benchmarked — Tested system performance under load to identify latency limits.
  • Integrated — Connected third-party APIs or microservices into a cohesive system.
  • Overhauled — Completely redesigned an ineffective application layer or codebase.
  • Debugged — Located and fixed critical production race conditions or memory leaks.

Example: Architected distributed event-driven microservices architecture using Apache Kafka, boosting transaction throughput by 420%. Review our real-world resume examples for engineering resume breakdowns.

3. Growth, Revenue & Marketing Power Verbs

Revenue-generating roles in sales, business development, performance marketing, and customer success demand verbs that highlight business expansion:

  • Accelerated — Fast-tracked customer acquisition cycles or pipeline velocity.
  • Captured — Won market share from competitors in high-friction enterprise accounts.
  • Monetized — Converted previously unpaid product engagement into paying ARR tiers.
  • Outperformed — Exceeded assigned quotas, benchmarks, or historic team targets.
  • Amplified — Multiplied brand reach, social engagement, or inbound marketing inquiries.
  • Doubled / Tripled — High-impact quantifiable expansion of sales pipelines or revenue.
  • Penetrated — Successfully entered new geographical or vertical industry markets.
  • Negotiated — Closed enterprise contracts with favorable commercial terms and margins.
  • Cultivated — Built long-term client partnerships that resulted in net-dollar expansion.
  • Converted — Turned cold prospects into active pipeline demos and paying accounts.

Example: Accelerated enterprise sales velocity from 90 to 52 days, closing $1.4M in new ACV across Fortune 500 fintech targets in FY2025.

4. Problem-Solving, Operations & Efficiency Power Verbs

Operations managers, project leaders, and supply chain analysts should choose verbs that demonstrate cost reduction, waste elimination, and process excellence:

  • Streamlined — Removed unnecessary procedural hurdles to accelerate execution speed.
  • Centralized — Unified fragmented documentation, vendor accounts, or data pipelines.
  • Eliminated — Completely removed recurring errors, manual dependencies, or budget waste.
  • Standardized — Implemented repeatable SOPs and compliance frameworks across regions.
  • Mitigated — Proactively prevented security risks, regulatory fines, or project delays.
  • Audited — Conducted rigorous inspections to ensure operational and financial compliance.
  • Rectified — Fixed operational deficiencies or logistical breakdowns under pressure.
  • Optimized — Fine-tuned workflows, inventory turns, or resource allocations for peak output.

Example: Streamlined vendor procurement approvals through automated workflows, reducing purchase order processing from 14 days to under 48 hours.

5. Research, Analytics & Data Science Power Verbs

Data scientists, financial analysts, and researchers should use verbs that describe scientific rigor, statistical validation, and business intelligence discovery:

  • Synthesized — Combined complex quantitative data points into clear executive recommendations.
  • Dissected — Analyzed root causes of user churn, funnel drop-off, or financial anomalies.
  • Forecasted — Built predictive econometric or regression models to guide quarterly budgets.
  • Modeled — Created machine learning algorithms or simulation engines.
  • Deciphered — Translated noisy telemetry logs into actionable product feature insights.
  • Quantified — Assigned concrete financial or metric value to qualitative operational risks.
  • Extracted — Pulled high-signal business intelligence from petabyte-scale data lakes.

Example: Forecasted customer lifetime value (LTV) using XGBoost models, allowing performance marketing teams to reallocate $250K in ad spend to high-margin cohorts. Learn how to highlight these in our guide on how to write resume bullet points that show impact.

5 Words to Immediately Delete from Your Resume

Certain phrases have been overused to the point of becoming visual white noise to hiring managers:

1. "Responsible for" — Describes an obligation, not an achievement. Replace with what you actually did (Delivered, Spearheaded).
2. "Assisted with" — Sounds passive and minimizes your contribution. Replace with Co-developed, Facilitated, or Researched.
3. "Hardworking / Motivated" — Show, don't tell. Let your quantified metrics prove your drive.
4. "Handled" — Vague and uninspiring. Did you resolve, negotiate, coordinate, or manage?
5. "Successfully" — Redundant. If an achievement is on your resume, success is already implied.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can strong action verbs help my resume pass ATS filters?

Yes. Modern ATS parsers utilize contextual entity recognition. Verbs like Architected, Implemented, and Negotiated indicate high professional seniority, boosting candidate ranking compared to passive phrasing.

What if I did not lead the project alone?

Use collaborative action verbs that still convey active ownership, such as Co-authored, Collaborated, Partnered, Contributed, or Co-designed. Avoid Assisted or Helped, which obscure your individual contribution.

How often should I vary my action verbs?

Never use the same action verb twice within the same role description. If your role involved leadership, rotate between Directed, Orchestrated, Guided, Mobilized, and Spearheaded.

Where can I check if my bullet points have the right keyword impact?
